metaDescription: USB-C hubs for MacBook compared on HDMI refresh rate, pass-through charging, port speeds and external display limits, so the extra ports do what you expect.
expertTake: The Anker 7-in-2 Mac hub is the best overall pick because it turns two of a MacBook's USB-C ports into a full set of ports while keeping 4K at 60 Hz HDMI and 100 W charging. The Hiearcool 7-in-1 is the value pick for office work where 4K at 30 Hz is acceptable. Anyone who needs two independent external monitors from a base M-series MacBook should skip these hubs, because Apple's base chips drive only one native external display.
introParagraphs: MacBooks ship with very few ports, so a USB-C hub is one of the first accessories most owners buy. The right hub depends less on the port count than on what the laptop can actually drive: how many displays, how much charging power and how fast the data ports run.

This guide compares hubs and docks chosen for MacBooks. We evaluated each on published specifications, display output, pass-through charging, port speeds and owner feedback patterns, and we point out where a hub cannot overcome a limit set by the laptop itself.

products.name: Anker 7-in-2 USB-C Hub for MacBook, 4K at 60 Hz HDMI, 100 W

specList.label: Connection
specList.value: Plugs into two MacBook USB-C ports

products.description:
The Anker 7-in-2 hub plugs into two of a MacBook's USB-C ports at once and turns them into a larger set of ports, including a multi-function USB-C port that supports charging up to 100 W. It offers HDMI at 4K and 60 Hz, which is the refresh rate you want for a desktop monitor. It is designed to sit tightly against the side of the laptop, which avoids the dangling cable of a conventional hub.

The two-port attachment is a design choice with a cost: it uses two of the laptop's ports to give you one multi-function port plus others. If your MacBook has only two ports, you effectively trade two ports for a larger set. Compared with the Anker 5-in-1, it adds 60 Hz video and a higher charging wattage. Compared with the Hiearcool, it doubles the HDMI refresh rate.

Setup is plug and go, with no drivers required. Check that your MacBook model supports the display you plan to use, since base M-series MacBooks drive one external display natively. The rigid body can stress the ports if you tug the laptop, so avoid heavy cables hanging off it. Aluminum-style hubs run warm under sustained load, which is normal.
products.bestFor: MacBook owners who want a 60 Hz 4K display and strong charging from a tight, direct-attach hub.
pros: HDMI at 4K and 60 Hz matches a desktop monitor refresh rate
Charging input up to 100 W suits MacBook Pro chargers
Direct-attach design avoids a dangling cable
Thunderbolt 4 compatible for modern MacBooks
cons: Uses two USB-C ports on the laptop
Rigid body can stress ports if bumped
Still limited by the MacBook's display support

products.name: Anker 5-in-1 USB-C Hub, 4K HDMI, 85 W Pass-Through
products.description:
The Anker 5-in-1 hub is a small traveling hub with a 4K HDMI output, one powered 5 Gbps USB-C data port, two 5 Gbps USB-A ports and 85 W pass-through charging. It is a compact, cabled hub that takes one laptop port and shares it among five connectors. The specs are modest and well matched to a typical MacBook Air.

The listing does not promise 60 Hz, so treat the HDMI as a 30 Hz output for 4K, which is fine for documents and video but less smooth for scrolling. Compared with the Anker 7-in-2, it is smaller and uses only one port, but it is less capable. Compared with the Hiearcool, it has a more established brand and a slightly lower charging ceiling.

Ownership is easy, though cabled hubs can pull on the laptop port if the cable is short. Keep the hub on the desk, not hanging. If you want the hub to stay put, use a laptop stand or a small cable clip. Power delivery of 85 W is enough for most MacBook Air and 14-inch MacBook Pro chargers, though a 16-inch MacBook Pro may charge slowly.
products.bestFor: Travelers and MacBook Air owners who want a small hub with 4K HDMI and pass-through charging.
pros: Compact hub with HDMI, USB-C and two USB-A ports
85 W pass-through suits most MacBook chargers
5 Gbps ports handle flash drives and card readers
Established brand with wide support
cons: Listing does not promise 60 Hz HDMI
Cabled body can tug at the laptop port

products.name: Hiearcool 7-in-1 USB-C Hub, 4K at 30 Hz HDMI, 100 W PD

specList.label: Ports
specList.value: Seven in total, including USB and card slots

products.description:
The Hiearcool is a seven-port dongle hub in a Space Gray finish that matches MacBook colors, offering HDMI at 4K and 30 Hz and power delivery up to 100 W. It is the low cost multiport hub in this guide.

The 30 Hz limit is the key spec. At 30 Hz, a 4K display refreshes half as often as a standard 60 Hz monitor, which makes cursor movement and scrolling feel a bit laggy. For static documents, spreadsheets and presentations, it is acceptable. Compared with the Anker 7-in-2, it is cheaper but less smooth for desktop use. Compared with the Berlat, it adds charging and HDMI.

In use, pay attention to heat and cable strain. Dongle hubs run warm, especially when charging and driving a monitor, and a lightly built body can flex. Plug USB drives in firmly, and keep it supported on the desk. If you need a smooth 4K desktop, step up to a hub that lists 60 Hz.
products.bestFor: Budget buyers who need HDMI, charging and ports for presentations and documents.
pros: Seven ports in one compact dongle at a low cost tier
Space Gray finish matches MacBook colors
Power delivery up to 100 W
HDMI handles presentations and documents
cons: 4K runs at only 30 Hz, so motion feels less smooth
Runs warm during charging and video output

products.name: Anker 8-in-1 USB-C Dock, Dual HDMI, 1 Gbps Ethernet, PD-In
products.description:
The Anker 8-in-1 dock has two HDMI ports, a 1 Gbps Ethernet port, two USB-A ports and a USB-C power-in port, with a captive cable to the laptop. It is the only hub here that aims at two monitors. The Ethernet port gives a stable wired connection for video calls and large downloads.

The MacBook caveat is important. Base Apple silicon MacBooks drive one external display natively, so a dual-HDMI dock may mirror a second monitor and not extend it unless the laptop has a Pro or Max chip or you add DisplayLink drivers. Compared with the Anker 7-in-2, it offers a second HDMI and Ethernet, but it will not give a second extended screen on a base MacBook. Compared with the 5-in-1, it is larger and needs its own power adapter.

Ownership requires attention to setup. Plug the dock's power adapter into the wall, confirm your MacBook model supports the number of displays you want and keep the cable out of the way. Docks run warm, and a captive cable is a failure point over years of daily plugging. If you only need one screen, a simpler hub is more reliable.
products.bestFor: MacBook Pro or Max owners who want two monitors and a wired network connection.
pros: Two HDMI ports for dual-monitor setups
1 Gbps Ethernet for a stable network
Separate USB-C power-in port keeps the laptop charged
Two USB-A ports for peripherals
cons: Base MacBooks may mirror the second screen
Captive cable and warm body are wear points

products.name: BERLAT 7-in-1 USB-C Hub, USB 3.0 and USB 2.0, Aluminum
products.description:
The Berlat hub offers one USB 3.0 port at 5 Gbps, four USB 2.0 ports and two USB-C 2.0 ports in an aluminum body, and it is the lowest cost hub in the lineup. It is aimed at connecting keyboards, mice, flash drives and other accessories. Most of its ports are USB 2.0, which runs at far lower speed than USB 3.0.

That speed gap is the key limit. USB 2.0 peaks at 480 Mbps, so it suits keyboards and mice but is a poor choice for external SSDs or fast card readers. Compared with the Xiaobi hub, it has fewer fast ports. Compared with the Anker models, it has no video output, so it will not drive a monitor.

Ownership is mostly about matching ports to devices. Put the one USB 3.0 port to work on a drive, and use the USB 2.0 ports for mice and keyboards. Check that the hub is aluminum body to spread heat. It is a low-risk way to add ports, but not a dock.
products.bestFor: Buyers who need many low-speed ports for keyboards, mice and drives at the lowest cost.
pros: Seven ports at the lowest cost tier
Aluminum body spreads heat
One USB 3.0 port for a drive
Suits keyboards, mice and accessories
cons: Most ports are USB 2.0 and slow
No pass-through charging for the laptop

products.name: Xiaobi 7-Port USB 3.0 Hub, 4 USB-A and 3 USB-C, 4 ft Cable
products.description:
The Xiaobi hub is a seven-port data hub with four USB-A and three USB-C ports at USB 3.0 speeds and a four-foot cable to the laptop. It is a pure data splitter: no video, no Ethernet and no listed charging for the laptop. The long cable lets you place it on a desk away from the laptop.

The use case is clear. If your accessories are drives, keyboards and cameras, a seven-port USB 3.0 hub does the job. Compared with the Berlat, it has faster ports across the board. Compared with the Anker docks, it cannot drive a monitor or charge the laptop, so it is an addition, not a replacement.

Ownership notes: powered versus unpowered matters, since multiple drives can exceed what a laptop port can supply. Keep high-draw devices on their own power. The long cable is a convenience but also a wear point where it flexes near the plug. Check the port layout to be sure large plugs do not block neighbors.
products.bestFor: Desk setups with many drives and accessories that need USB 3.0 speeds.
pros: Seven USB 3.0 ports across USB-A and USB-C
Four-foot cable lets you place it on the desk
Handles drives, cameras and keyboards
Low to mid cost tier
cons: Several drives may exceed port power

buyingCriteria.explanation: No hub can exceed what the laptop's chip supports. Base M-series MacBooks drive one external display natively, so a dual-HDMI dock like the Anker 8-in-1 may mirror instead of extend. Pro and Max chips support more displays. Check your model's spec page before buying a hub for a second monitor.

4K at 30 Hz, as on the Hiearcool, is fine for documents but looks choppy when scrolling or moving a cursor. 4K at 60 Hz, as on the Anker 7-in-2, is the desktop standard. Many cheap hubs list 4K but quietly run at 30 Hz, so read the refresh rate and not just the resolution.

The hub takes a share of the power for itself, so a listed 85 W or 100 W maximum may deliver less to the laptop. The Anker 5-in-1 lists 85 W pass-through and the Anker 7-in-2 lists up to 100 W. A MacBook Air is happy with less, while a 16-inch MacBook Pro may charge slowly under load. Use the charger that came with the laptop where possible.

USB 3.0 runs at 5 Gbps and USB 2.0 at 480 Mbps. The Berlat has four USB 2.0 ports, while the Xiaobi and Anker hubs run at USB 3.0 speeds. Plug external SSDs into fast ports, and keep slow ports for keyboards and mice. Mixed hubs surprise buyers who plug a drive into the wrong port.

A direct-attach hub like the Anker 7-in-2 sits against the laptop and avoids a cable, but it uses two ports and can stress them. A cabled hub like the Hiearcool or Xiaobi puts less strain on the ports and can sit on the desk. Choose by how you work: on a desk, a cabled hub is easy, and on the go, a rigid one is neat.

Dongle hubs run warm when driving video and charging. Aluminum bodies, as on the Berlat, spread heat better than thin plastic. A hub that runs very hot can throttle or drop the display. Pick a hub with a metal body if you plan to keep it plugged in all day.

specDecoder.watchFor: The Anker 7-in-2 lists 60 Hz and the Hiearcool lists 30 Hz.

specDecoder.meaning: The maximum charging power the hub can send to the laptop, after the hub takes its own share.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Anker 5-in-1 lists 85 W and the Hiearcool lists 100 W power delivery.

specDecoder.meaning: USB 3.0 transfers data about ten times faster than USB 2.0. Speed matters for drives and card readers.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Berlat has four USB 2.0 ports and one USB 3.0 port.

A USB-C port that accepts a power adapter to charge the laptop through the dock.

howWeEvaluated.title: Display capability
howWeEvaluated.description: We started with HDMI refresh rate and display count, such as 60 Hz on the Anker 7-in-2 and 30 Hz on the Hiearcool. We noted MacBook display limits. Our scores are editorial assessments based on published specifications and owner feedback patterns.

howWeEvaluated.title: Charging
howWeEvaluated.description: We read pass-through wattage, from 85 W on the Anker 5-in-1 to 100 W on the Anker 7-in-2 and Hiearcool, and noted that the hub takes some power.

howWeEvaluated.title: Port speeds and mix
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared USB 3.0 and USB 2.0 ports and what each suits, such as the mixed Berlat and the all-3.0 Xiaobi.

howWeEvaluated.title: Design and heat
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered direct-attach, cabled and captive-cable designs and aluminum bodies. Owner feedback about heat and strain shaped the cautions.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value and honesty
howWeEvaluated.description: We judged each hub by relative cost tier and avoided price figures. The Berlat was judged as a basic port expander, not a dock.

cards.label: Hub
cards.text: The Anker 5-in-1, Anker 7-in-2 and Hiearcool are compact, travel-friendly and need no wall power.

cards.label: Dock
cards.text: The Anker 8-in-1 adds dual HDMI and Ethernet and needs its own power adapter, suited to a fixed desk.

howToChoose.note: Choose a hub if you travel. Choose a dock if you work at one desk with two monitors.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: HDMI at 60 Hz, charging wattage that matches your charger, fast ports for drives and a note on how many displays your chip supports.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Anker 7-in-2 leads on desktop use, the 5-in-1 on travel and the 8-in-1 on dual monitors.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You use an external monitor daily and want 60 Hz, steady charging and a trusted brand. The Anker 7-in-2 pays back in comfort.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You need extra USB ports for peripherals. The Berlat or Xiaobi covers that at a low cost.

maintenance.why: Lint and dust build up in USB-C ports and cause poor contact. Blow out gently and wipe the plug.
Hubs run warm when charging and driving video. If it gets too hot to touch, unplug and give it space.
Cable strain damages ports and captive cables. Keep the hub on the desk and the cable relaxed.
Display and wake issues are often fixed by updates. Check the maker's page for firmware.
If the laptop discharges while plugged in, use a higher-wattage charger or connect power directly.

faq.q: Will a hub give me two monitors on my MacBook?
faq.a: Only if the MacBook chip supports it. Base M-series MacBooks drive one external display natively, so a dual-HDMI dock may mirror the second screen.
The hub may be limited to 30 Hz at 4K. Look for a hub that lists 60 Hz, and check the cable and the monitor setting.

faq.q: Do hubs slow down my drive?
faq.a: They can if the drive sits on a USB 2.0 port or shares bandwidth. Use a USB 3.0 port and check the hub's port speeds.

faq.q: Can I charge my MacBook through the hub?
faq.a: Yes, with a pass-through charging hub. The hub keeps some power, so use a charger with enough wattage.

faq.q: Is Thunderbolt 4 compatible the same as Thunderbolt 4?
faq.a: No. It means the hub works with a Thunderbolt 4 port, not that it delivers Thunderbolt speeds.
Yes, especially when charging and driving a monitor. Metal bodies spread heat better, but a very hot hub should be unplugged.
